title: Judge the sorter by its curve
allegory: Comparing control protocols is like comparing apple sorters: turn any sorter's dial and it trades rotten apples shipped against good apples binned, so the fair comparison is each sorter's whole curve, and a sorter beaten on both counts at once is never worth buying.
map: a shipment with not one rotten apple in it
safety: P(zero backdoors submitted over the whole run | the red team's attack)
good apples that reach the customer
usefulness: fraction of correct code under honest U, scaled so T = 0 and U = 1
the protocol's knob: audit budget, defer or edit threshold
cutting out the bruise instead of binning the apple
trusted editing: T removes suspicious lines and keeps U's algorithm
the sorters no other sorter beats on both counts
the Pareto frontier; every point inside it is dominated

cap.1: 'My sorter ships zero rotten apples!' It also bins every apple. Being perfectly safe is easy if you give up on being useful.
cap.2: Never submit anything and you are perfectly safe; submit everything and you are perfectly useful. A protocol's safety means nothing without its usefulness beside it.
cap.3: Safety = P(zero backdoors submitted over the run | attack policy); usefulness = P(submitted code correct | U honest). Each alone has a trivial optimum, so neither alone can rank protocols.

cap.1: Turn the sorter's dial stricter and fewer rotten apples ship, but more good ones hit the bin. Every setting is one point; sweep the dial and you get a curve.
cap.2: Protocols have dials too: the audit budget, and the suspicion threshold above which you defer to or edit with the trusted model. Sweeping them traces safety against usefulness.
cap.3: ARENA's simulate_safety fits clean and backdoored suspicion distributions, resamples runs of any length at any backdoor rate, and sweeps the defer threshold and audit budget: a frontier, not a point.

chapters.name: Four sorters, one axis
chapters.title: Safety (%) by protocol, one dial setting each (Greenblatt et al.)

cap.1: Hand-check only the first crates: 15% safe. A scanner plus spot checks on the worst: 62%. Swap in your own apples when unsure: 83%. Cut the bruises out: 92%.
cap.2: Upfront auditing audits the first submissions; trusted monitoring audits the top 2% by suspicion; defer-to-trusted swaps in T's code above a threshold; trusted editing has T cut suspicious lines.
cap.3: Greenblatt, Shlegeris, Sachan and Roger (Redwood Research, ICML 2024): APPS problems, an untrusted model inserting backdoors. Safety alone is half the picture; each bar hides a usefulness cost.

chapters.name: Draw the frontier
chapters.note: not to scale: right = more useful, up = safer

nodes.label: only T: safe, no U work

cap.1: Plot each sorter by safety and by work kept. At 92% safe, swapping keeps 83% of the work and cutting bruises keeps 94%. Swapping is simply beaten.
cap.2: A point is dominated when another is at least as good on both axes and better on one. Join the unbeaten points: that line is the Pareto frontier. Anything inside it buys safety at a worse price.
cap.3: At matched 92% safety, trusted editing beats defer-to-trusted by 11 points of usefulness: T can cut a suspicious fragment far more reliably than it can write a correct APPS solution from scratch.

chapters.name: Your frontier flatters you

left.title: the plot you first make
lines: threshold tuned on the same data
a red team that always attacks

right.title: the plot you can defend

chapters.verdict: A frontier drawn against a weak adversary is a frontier against a weak adversary.

cap.1: Your first plot flatters you: you tuned the sorter on the same apples you tested it on, against a cheat who never gets clever. Real cheats hide their rot.
cap.2: Two quiet inflations: a suspicion threshold chosen on the evaluation data, which overstates usefulness, and a fixed always-attack red team where the paper optimises the attack per protocol.
cap.3: Against trusted monitoring the best response is to attack only on unusually good backdoor opportunities, and safety falls sharply. Split calibration from evaluation, let the red team learn, state your normalisation.

chapters.name: Choose on the curve
items: Sweep each dial: a curve, not a dot
Beaten on both? Never pick it

cap.1: Deploying a model you do not fully trust is a choice on this curve. Knowing the whole curve lets you steer that choice, not trust one flattering number.
cap.2: Report every protocol as a curve over its dial, and compare at matched safety or matched usefulness. Then the question is which point you want, not which protocol 'wins'.
cap.3: For steering AI: control assumes the model may be subverting you and asks what you can still guarantee. The frontier is that guarantee's price list, and its ordering held even on a few tens of problems.

coda.title: Sweep the dial, draw the curve: deferring vs editing (toy)

params.label: monitor sharpness (how far backdoors stand out)
chance an edit removes the backdoor
dial: share of submissions sent to T

caption.1: Across: work kept. Up: safety. Each curve is one protocol with its dial swept; higher at equal usefulness wins. Sharpen the monitor, then make edits sloppier.
caption.2: Toy: audit the top 2% by suspicion, send the next slice to T. Deferring swaps in T's weaker code; editing keeps U's algorithm but may miss the backdoor. Editing wins wherever you keep most of the work.
caption.3: Safety is c/(c + b): caught at audit versus backdoor submitted, in the many-attack limit, with logistic stand-ins for the suspicion distributions. Defaults sit near the paper's points, but trust only the shapes.

where_else: Classifiers: precision against recall, a curve over the threshold rather than one accuracy
Medical screening: catching disease against false alarms, the ROC curve
Finance: the efficient frontier of risk against return

hamming.what: A plot of every control protocol as a point (chance of zero backdoors over a run against useful work kept) with the unbeaten points joined into a frontier.
hamming.when: Whenever you compare ways to deploy a model you do not fully trust, or tune one protocol's dial such as the audit budget or the defer or edit threshold.
hamming.why: Any single number can be gamed (submit nothing and you are perfectly safe), so only the curve, measured against the red team's best attack, shows which protocol buys safety most cheaply.

object.title: The frontier board
object.subtitle: Every protocol is a small cloud of Monte-Carlo estimates: right is more useful work kept, up is safer.

clusters.label: only T: perfectly safe, none of U's work

cap.1: Every protocol is a dot. Right: more useful work kept. Up: safer. The green line joins the dots nothing beats; that line is the frontier.
cap.2: Coordinates are (usefulness, safety). Frontier points are non-dominated: no other protocol is at least as good on both axes and better on one.
cap.3: Each dot is really a small cloud: ARENA estimates safety by Monte-Carlo resampling of suspicion scores on a few tens of problems, so each coordinate has sampling noise.

cap.1: Look along the top: deferring and editing are equally safe, but editing keeps far more of the work. Deferring is off the line, so never pick it at that setting.
cap.2: At 92% safety, defer-to-trusted keeps 83% usefulness and trusted editing 94%. Same safety, eleven points more work: defer is dominated.
cap.3: Routing on the easier capability wins: T edits a local perturbation out of U's working code far better than it authors a correct solution itself.

cap.1: Down the right edge: both ship the strong model's own code, but checking the most suspicious beats checking the first few by a mile.
cap.2: Both submit U's code, so both keep nearly all the useful work; monitoring is 62% safe against upfront auditing's 15%.
cap.3: Upfront auditing loses to a red team that simply waits: the audit budget is spent on the first submissions and everything afterwards is accepted.

cap.1: From above, the board is flat: two numbers per protocol, no more. Whatever you report, report both.
cap.2: A protocol's dial moves its dot along a curve of its own; the frontier is the upper-right envelope of all those curves.
cap.3: These coordinates are against one attack policy. Against each protocol's best response the dots slide down; for trusted monitoring, sharply.

predict.q: A protocol never submits the untrusted model's code. Where does it sit?

options.t: Perfectly safe and none of U's usefulness

predict.why: No U code means no backdoor can ever land: safety 100%. But usefulness is scaled so T alone scores 0, so it keeps none of what U adds. Safe and useless, which is why one number lies.

predict.q: Deferring and editing both reach 92% safety. Deferring keeps 83% of the useful work, editing 94%. Which is dominated?

options.t: Editing, because it keeps more of U's code

predict.why: Dominated means at least as bad on both axes and worse on one. Deferring ties on safety and loses on usefulness, so there is no reason to choose it at that setting.

predict.q: Your frontier puts trusted editing on top. What should you check before calling the ranking settled?

options.t: Held-out threshold calibration and a red team that adapts
More decimal places on each point
Whether the plot's colours match the paper

predict.why: A threshold tuned on the evaluation data overstates usefulness, and a fixed attack overstates safety. Report the frontier under the strongest attack you managed.

object.where: Any trade-off you tune with a threshold: precision against recall, screening against false alarms, risk against return.
